angles.drive: Loving a race is how you love the work. Water comes in slowly for you and nothing refills it like someone to beat, and you put the race ahead of the task. Keep a rival you like, and the race stays a game worth running.

You jump in first and ask about the depth afterwards. Waiting at the side feels worse to you than being wrong, and you go first instead of going sure. Keep jumping, and bring one person who checks the depth before you.

You go all in together or you do not go in. A shared risk feels lighter than one carried alone, and you pool first and sort out shares later. Name your part before you go in, and you keep both the partner and the money.

You race in secret, under cover of being friendly. Being seen to want the win feels more dangerous than wanting it, so you race quietly rather than openly. Remember that you get no credit for a race you kept hidden.

You spend shared money like shared time, freely and without counting. Because pooled money feels like yours to move, you pay for the group ahead of counting your part. Hold on to the fact that part of what you spend was a friend's.

You never have enough, and you are mostly honest about it. Wanting beats having for you, and you reach for the next shared venture ahead of settling what the last one paid. You decide where the race ends, and that line is not drawn.

Rivalry wakes you up. A competitor in the water and your stroke sharpens, your pace lifts, and the race becomes the point of the day. You measure yourself against real people, openly, and you move faster for it than any plan could make you.

Your nerves hold exactly when the other side hopes they will not. The staring contest of a negotiation, the final round, the moment someone raises the stakes to scare you: your pulse spikes and your voice does not. Opponents read calm. It is actually appetite.

Mid-contest, you change course faster than anyone can cover you. The blocked route becomes a new route, the lost argument becomes a different argument, and by the time a rival adjusts, you have moved twice more. Beating you requires predicting you. Nobody manages it consistently.

Your competitiveness works underground. The compliment with a current in it, the help that arrives slightly late, the praise for a rival delivered where it does maximum quiet damage. On the surface, all is warmth. Below, the sand is always moving under someone.

Other people’s tides hurt you. The friend’s windfall, the peer’s launch, the sibling’s easy luck: each lands somewhere unprotected, and your congratulations come out slightly waterlogged. You want the good things wanted. You just want them to arrive in your harbor first.

Commitments run off you when conditions change, and conditions always change. The agreement meant everything at signing and less at settlement, the story adjusts to its audience, and blame finds you already moved downstream. Nothing sticks, which was once an advantage. People notice what nothing sticks to.
